werk/metallica-kill-em-all.text:
Metallica was formed in Los Angeles in 1981 by Lars Ulrich and James Hetfield. The band moved to San Francisco to get bassist Cliff Burton. The demo No Life 'til Leather caught the attention of Jon Zazula, who started the label Megaforce Records and put up 15,000 dollars for the recording. Guitarist Dave Mustaine, who co-wrote some of the songs, was fired shortly before the recording and replaced by Kirk Hammett. In May 1983 the band recorded the album with producer Paul Curcio in Rochester, New York. The title Metal Up Your Ass was changed on Zazula's advice.

The album brought a faster and more aggressive style than the rock music of the early 1980s. Whiplash and Jump in the Fire were the singles. It was well received on release and is now regarded as groundbreaking for thrash metal. It inspired later bands.
werk/metallica-kill-em-all.listen: In Whiplash, listen to the tempo and to how tightly the guitars and drums play together. Notice the energy in the vocals.

werk/metallica-load.text:
After the success of the 1991 album Metallica, the group toured for years. In early 1994 the members went their separate ways, and Lars Ulrich even went to court to get out of the contract with Elektra. Hetfield and Ulrich then worked on demos in Ulrich's basement studio. Recording began in May 1995 in Sausalito, with producer Bob Rock. It went so smoothly that almost thirty tracks were ready. Half of them appeared on Load, the rest a year later on Reload.

On Load the members left their thrash metal roots for a hard rock sound with influences from southern rock, blues rock, country rock and grunge. The lyrics are more personal and reflective. Fans criticised the new sound and the new look, with short hair, leather jackets and make-up. Even so, Load was a great success. Until It Sleeps became the first and only American top ten hit. The reviews were mixed. Later reviewers find the album too long.
werk/metallica-load.listen: Listen to Until It Sleeps and notice how it sounds like hard rock rather than thrash. Can you hear the personal tone of the lyrics?

werk/metallica-master-of-puppets.text:
After Kill 'Em All and Ride the Lightning, Metallica wanted to make an album that would win over critics and fans. The group recorded Master of Puppets from September to December 1985 at Sweet Silence Studios in Copenhagen, with producer Flemming Rasmussen. The musicians deliberately chose against the slick production and the synthesizers of glam metal and stayed sober on recording days. The sleeve shows a graveyard full of crosses on strings, moved by two hands.

The album was released on 3 March 1986 on Elektra Records. Instead of a single or video, an American tour with Ozzy Osbourne followed. During it, bassist Cliff Burton died on 27 September 1986 in a bus accident in Sweden. Critics praised the music and the political lyrics. The album is regarded as one of the most influential metal records and as the record that consolidated American thrash metal. In 2015 the Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry, the first metal album to be included.
werk/metallica-master-of-puppets.listen: Listen to Battery and notice how the acoustic opening turns into a fast, hard guitar part. See whether you can hear how tightly the band locks the riffs together.

werk/metallica-metallica.text:
Metallica, known as The Black Album, is the fifth album by the band of the same name and was released in August 1991 on Elektra. James Hetfield and Lars Ulrich wrote the songs in two months in 1990. As producer the band chose Bob Rock, whose work for Mötley Crüe had made an impression. Recording took eight months, mainly at One on One Recording Studios in Los Angeles, and often ended in arguments with Rock. He had the group play more as a unit and sought a live feel.

The sound became slower, heavier and more polished than on the thrash metal records before it, although traces of thrash remained. Enter Sandman, The Unforgiven, Nothing Else Matters, Wherever I May Roam and Sad but True were released as singles. The album received wide praise, spent four weeks at number 1 on the American chart and became the band's best-selling album, with more than thirty million copies worldwide.
werk/metallica-metallica.listen: In Enter Sandman, listen to the heavy guitar riff with which the song opens and to how the rhythm grows ever tighter afterwards.

werk/metallica-reload.text:
Reload was released on 18 November 1997, as the follow-up to Load. Both records come from the same sessions with producer Bob Rock at The Plant Studios in Sausalito, between May 1995 and February 1996. Metallica first thought of a double album, but with almost thirty tracks the band decided to split the material. Extra recording sessions followed in 1997. It is the last studio album with bassist Jason Newsted.

The sound stays far from the thrash metal of the past: hard rock with influences from blues, country and grunge. Kirk Hammett played rhythm guitar on one of the band's albums for the first time. Marianne Faithfull sings on The Memory Remains, the first guest female vocalist on a studio album by the band. The Unforgiven II is the first sequel to one of their own songs. The reviews were mixed: some praised the playing, others missed innovation.
werk/metallica-reload.listen: Listen to Low Man's Lyric and notice the hurdy-gurdy and the violin, instruments you would not readily expect from a metal band.

werk/metallica-ride-the-lightning.text:
Ride the Lightning is Metallica's second studio album and was released on 27 July 1984 on Megaforce Records. The band recorded the album in three weeks at Sweet Silence Studios in Copenhagen, with producer Flemming Rasmussen. Because Megaforce could not bear the costs, the European label Music for Nations paid for the studio. The title comes from The Stand by Stephen King, in which it refers to the electric chair. On the sleeve, lightning strikes from the band logo into such a chair.

The album remains thrash metal, but goes beyond the fast debut Kill 'Em All. Bassist Cliff Burton brought music theory with him and contributed more to the writing. There are acoustic guitars, long instrumental passages and richer harmonies. Fade to Black is a ballad about suicide that begins with an acoustic guitar and grows steadily heavier and faster. Critics found the record more ambitious than the previous one, and it later became a lasting influence on thrash metal.
werk/metallica-ride-the-lightning.listen: Listen to Fade to Black and notice how the song begins with an acoustic guitar and gradually becomes heavier and faster.

werk/metallica-st-anger.text:
In January 2001 Metallica turned an old army barracks in San Francisco into a studio. Bassist Jason Newsted left shortly afterwards, so producer Bob Rock played the bass himself. In July 2001 James Hetfield entered a rehab clinic, as a result of which recording only resumed in 2002. Two filmmakers followed the band for the documentary Some Kind of Monster.

The result sounds raw. The guitars are tuned lower, the production has not been smoothed over and there are no guitar solos, because according to Kirk Hammett they sounded like an afterthought. The title song won a Grammy for Best Metal Performance in 2004. The record received mixed reviews, but did go straight to number 1 in the United States.
werk/metallica-st-anger.listen: Listen to St. Anger and notice the drum sound and the absence of a guitar solo. Can you hear four people playing together in one room?

werk/mgmt-oracular-spectacular.text:
MGMT became a duo of Andrew VanWyngarden and Ben Goldwasser, who in March and April 2007 were in the studio with producer Dave Fridmann for their major-label debut. Time to Pretend and Kids had already appeared on an EP and were re-recorded. The album was released in October 2007 on RED Ink and in January 2008 physically on Columbia. The band played live as a five-piece.

The music is synth-pop that critics praised for its production, direction and make-up. Time to Pretend, Electric Feel and Kids were the singles. An AllMusic reviewer called the songs the catchiest pop songs from New York since the turn of the century. NME named it best album of 2008 and it was nominated for a Brit Award. In 2009 Rolling Stone placed it at number 18 among the best albums of the decade.
werk/mgmt-oracular-spectacular.listen: In Electric Feel, listen to the synthesizers that carry the song. Notice how catchy the melody is.

werk/michael-jackson-bad.text:
After the enormous success of Thriller, Michael Jackson was under greater pressure than ever. He worked on the follow-up from 1985 to 1987, again with producer Quincy Jones, for the third and last time. Jones encouraged him to write more himself and to make an honest album. Jackson wrote almost all the songs. He wrote about sixty songs and recorded thirty-three, but Jones kept it to eleven.

The sound is harder and sharper, with digital synthesizers such as the Fairlight and the Synclavier, plus influences from hard rock and funk. Man in the Mirror came from Siedah Garrett and Glen Ballard, and Garrett sings on I Just Can't Stop Loving You. The album yielded a record five number one hits on the Hot 100, including Bad and Dirty Diana. Critics praised the singing and the arrangements, although some felt it did not match Thriller. It was the best-selling album of 1987 and 1988.
werk/michael-jackson-bad.listen: Listen to Bad and notice whether you can hear the digital synthesizers and the solid, sharp production that make this track sound harder.

werk/michael-jackson-ben.text:
Ben is Michael Jackson's second solo album for Motown, released on 4 August 1972, when he was still a member of the Jackson 5. Recording ran from November 1971 to February 1972. Berry Gordy was executive producer and six people produced the record.

The title song, the theme from the film Ben, became his first number 1 in the United States, won a Golden Globe and received an Oscar nomination. He also sings covers of My Girl, People Make the World Go Round, You Can Cry on My Shoulder and Shoo-Be-Doo-Be-Doo-Da-Day. The critics were mixed to positive. Rolling Stone thought it a good deal stronger than the first album.
werk/michael-jackson-ben.listen: In Ben, listen to the slow tempo of the song and to how much feeling there is in the singing.

werk/michael-jackson-forever-michael.text:
Forever, Michael was released on 16 January 1975 and was the last album Michael Jackson made at Motown. He was sixteen and, for the first time, sang as a tenor rather than as a boy soprano. Most of the tracks were recorded in 1974, but the release was pushed back because the success of the Jackson 5's Dancing Machine took precedence. The producers were Eddie Holland, Brian Holland, Hal Davis, Freddie Perren and Sam Brown III.

The sound is smoother and more grown-up, with soul and funk. We're Almost There and Just a Little Bit of You became singles. Robert Christgau gave the album an A minus and called One Day In Your Life a sure hit. Other critics felt the arrangements still sounded much like old Motown.
werk/michael-jackson-forever-michael.listen: Listen to One Day In Your Life and notice how calm and mature the voice sounds in this ballad.

werk/michael-jackson-got-to-be-there.text:
Got to Be There is Michael Jackson's first solo album, released by Motown on 24 January 1972, four weeks after the Jackson 5's Greatest Hits. Berry Gordy was executive producer. The arrangers included The Corporation, Gene Page and James Anthony Carmichael.

The album contains covers of Ain't No Sunshine, You've Got a Friend and Love Is Here and Now You're Gone. The tempo ranges from 74 beats per minute in Ain't No Sunshine to 170 in Rockin' Robin. The title song and Rockin' Robin became two big hits. AllMusic found the album as a whole uneven, but praised the covers of You've Got a Friend and Ain't No Sunshine as proof of his versatility as a singer.
werk/michael-jackson-got-to-be-there.listen: In Rockin' Robin, listen to the fast tempo and to how light and playful the singing is.

werk/michael-jackson-music-en-me.text:
Music & Me, Michael Jackson's third studio album, was released on 13 April 1973 on Motown. He was fourteen and his voice was beginning to change. He wanted to contribute his own songs and play instruments himself, but Motown did not allow it. Later he complained about this to his father, who eventually arranged the move to Epic Records. Because he was on a world tour with his brothers, promotion was limited. Stevie Wonder's With a Child's Heart was released as a single and reached number 50 on the Billboard Hot 100.

The reviews were favourable. AllMusic found the production and the arrangements routine, whereas Entertainment Weekly praised the vulnerable performance of With a Child's Heart. It is his lowest-selling album.
werk/michael-jackson-music-en-me.listen: Listen to With a Child's Heart and notice how vulnerable the young singer's voice sounds.

werk/michael-jackson-off-the-wall.text:
In the 1970s Michael Jackson had made several solo records at Motown, but control lay elsewhere. For his fifth album, the first at Epic Records, he wanted freedom and not a record that sounded like the Jacksons. Quincy Jones, with whom he had worked on the film The Wiz, produced. Stevie Wonder, Paul McCartney and Rod Temperton, among others, worked on the songs, and Jackson wrote three himself.

Off the Wall blends disco, pop, funk, R&B and ballads. Five singles were released. Don't Stop 'Til You Get Enough and Rock with You became number ones in America, and with four top ten singles from one album, Jackson was the first solo artist to achieve that. The sleeve with the tuxedo and socks became a trademark. The album was seen as a reintroduction and was a breakthrough.
werk/michael-jackson-off-the-wall.listen: Listen to the percussion in Don't Stop 'Til You Get Enough. His brother Randy played it.

werk/michael-jackson-thriller.text:
Thriller was made in 1982 at Westlake Recording Studios in Los Angeles, under producer Quincy Jones, who had also made Off the Wall. Michael Jackson wanted a record on which every track could be a hit. They recorded thirty songs, of which nine made it onto the album. Recording began with The Girl Is Mine, together with Paul McCartney.

The sound is post-disco and synth-pop with influences from funk and rock. For Beat It, Jones brought in Eddie Van Halen for the guitar solo. In Thriller, the actor Vincent Price speaks the closing line. With Billie Jean, Jones wanted to shorten the long intro, but Jackson insisted on keeping it because it made him want to dance. Billie Jean and Beat It topped the Hot 100. Seven singles reached the top ten, a record for a single album. The videos turned music videos into a serious art form. The album won eight Grammys and is regarded as the best-selling album of all time.
werk/michael-jackson-thriller.listen: Listen to the opening of Billie Jean and notice how long the intro lasts before the vocals begin, and how the bass line already sets the song in motion.

werk/michael-mcdonald-if-that-s-what-it-.text:
If That's What It Takes is the debut album by the American singer Michael McDonald, released on 3 August 1982 by Warner Bros. Records. Ted Templeman and Lenny Waronker produced the record. Lee Herschberg, Donn Landee and Jim Isaacson recorded the basic tracks, and Bobby Hata mastered the whole at Warner Bros. Recording Studios. The album has ten tracks, including the title track, Playin' By the Rules and Believe In It. It was the first of his solo albums.

The album reached number 6 on the Billboard 200. The single I Keep Forgettin (Every Time You're Near) reached number 4 on the Hot 100, and I Gotta Try number 44.
werk/michael-mcdonald-if-that-s-what-it-.listen: In I Keep Forgettin (Every Time You're Near), listen to the vocals, because this became the album's biggest single.

werk/michael-mcdonald-no-lookin-back.text:
No Lookin' Back is Michael McDonald's second solo studio album, released on 12 August 1985 by Warner Bros. Records, three years after If That's What It Takes. It was his last album with that company. For the first time he co-produced himself, together with Ted Templeman, and wrote or co-wrote all the songs. The guitarists Joe Walsh, Robben Ford and David Pack played on it, Jeff Porcaro sat behind the drums, Willie Weeks played bass and Cornelius Bumpus blew the horns. The title single, co-written by Kenny Loggins, reached number 34 on the Hot 100.

The reviews were mostly favourable, although Rolling Stone wrote scathingly about the singer's limited voice. Music Week, by contrast, heard impressive soul singing, close to Hall & Oates. The album reached number 45 on the Billboard 200.
werk/michael-mcdonald-no-lookin-back.listen: In No Lookin' Back, the first single, listen to how the vocals carry the song.

werk/michael-nyman-and-do-they-do-zoo-ca.text:
And Do They Do / Zoo Caprices is Michael Nyman's eighth album and his fifth with his own band. It combines two works. And Do They Do is a modern dance production commissioned by Siobhan Davies and the London Contemporary Dance Theatre, which premiered on 25 November 1986 at Sadler's Wells Theatre. It consists of four linked Songs, although nobody sings in it. The third is jazzy in colour, but based on Nachtlied by Robert Schumann.

He wrote Zoo Caprices for the violinist Alexander Balanescu, who played it in Paris in April 1986. It is an arrangement of the music for the film A Zed & Two Noughts by Peter Greenaway, in which Balanescu uses multiple stopping on a single violin to sound several harmonies at once. The record first appeared on LP on Ter Records, followed by the CD in 1989.
werk/michael-nyman-and-do-they-do-zoo-ca.listen: Listen to And Do They Do: Song III and try to hear, behind the jazzy colour, the kinship with Schumann's Nachtlied.

werk/michael-nyman-the-kiss-and-other-mo.text:
The Kiss and Other Movements is Michael Nyman's sixth album and the fifth he recorded with the Michael Nyman Band. The title song is an operatic duet between Dagmar Krause and Omar Ebrahim, based on a painting by Paul Richards that appears on the sleeve. Krause took over the role from Anne Pigalle and gave the piece a darker sound.

The album is a collection of varied pieces. Nose-List Song comes from the unfinished opera Tristram Shandy and was written for the soprano Sarah Leonard, to a text from the book by Laurence Sterne. Images Were Introduced comes from Memorial, made for a film by Peter Greenaway. Water Dances is the music for his film Making a Splash about synchronised swimming, in the version used for the film.
werk/michael-nyman-the-kiss-and-other-mo.listen: Listen to Nose-List Song and notice how the vocal part stays largely on a single note, while the instruments carry the musical ideas.

werk/michael-nyman-the-piano.text:
The Piano is the music for the film of the same name from 1993, released by Virgin Records and the twentieth album by the composer Michael Nyman. Strictly speaking it is not a recording from the film, but a partial re-recording of the score. In the film the actress Holly Hunter plays the piano; on the record the composer does so himself, with the Munich Philharmonic Orchestra under his direction and saxophonists from his own band. The best-known theme, The Heart Asks Pleasure First, is based on a Scottish song.

The record was nominated for a Golden Globe and a BAFTA, but lost to the music for Heaven & Earth and Schindler's List. The reception was mixed: AllMusic found the music subtle and beautiful, but also a little pale, whereas Entertainment Weekly felt that the score works better in the film than on disc.
werk/michael-nyman-the-piano.listen: Listen to The Heart Asks Pleasure First, the best-known theme from the film, and notice the melody of the Scottish song on which it is based.

werk/michael-rother-fernwarme.text:
Fernwärme is the fourth studio album by the German solo musician Michael Rother and was released in 1982 on Polydor. He recorded it in 1981 at his own Flammende Herzen Studio in Forst. It was his first album without Conny Plank, with whom he had made almost all of his work. It was also the last time for drummer Jaki Liebezeit: he played on the first four solo albums. Rother played the rest himself, on guitar and electronics. On later records he mainly used drum machines, although that can already be heard on this album.

The singles were Silberstreif and Hohe Luft. Silberstreif is the first track on the album. In some English-speaking countries the record was released under the title Silver Streak. Most critics reacted positively.
werk/michael-rother-fernwarme.listen: Listen to Silberstreif, the opening track. Notice the interplay of guitar, electronics and drums.

werk/michael-rother-flammende-herzen.text:
Flammende Herzen is the debut album by the German musician Michael Rother and was released in March 1977. He had previously made five records, with Neu! and Klaus Dinger and with Harmonia. Rother recorded the album from June to September 1976 at Conny's Studio with Conny Plank, who had also produced Neu! and Harmonia. Jaki Liebezeit of Can plays drums.

Rother played everything else himself: guitar, bass, electric piano, organ, synthesizer and electronic percussion. Unlike with his groups, the record is entirely instrumental and he plays most of the melodies on guitar. The album has five tracks, including the title song and Karussell, which came out together on a single. A year later the music was used for the film Flaming Hearts. Most critics reacted positively.
werk/michael-rother-flammende-herzen.listen: Listen to Flammende Herzen and notice the guitar melody above the steady rhythm of the drums.

werk/michael-rother-katzenmusik.text:
Katzenmusik is the third studio album by the German solo musician Michael Rother and was released in 1979. He recorded it between March and July of that year, at his own studio in Forst and at Conny's Studio. As on his first two records, he worked with producer Conny Plank, for the last time. Jaki Liebezeit of Can plays drums. Everything else he played himself, on guitar and electronics.

He limited his instruments and wrote the album as a suite in two parts. They are not separate songs, but twelve pieces: variations on four five-note melodies that keep returning. Most critics were positive. AllMusic called it one of his best works.
werk/michael-rother-katzenmusik.listen: Listen to Katzenmusik 9, the album's single. Notice the five-note melody that keeps returning.

werk/michael-rother-sterntaler.text:
Sterntaler is the second solo album by the German musician Michael Rother. It was recorded from September to November 1977, at his own studio in Forst and at Conny's Studio, and released in 1978 on Sky Records. As on his debut, he worked with Conny Plank, and Jaki Liebezeit of Can played drums.

Rother played almost everything himself: guitar, including Hawaiian slide guitar, piano, bass, vibraphone, synthesizer and strings. On a number of pieces, especially the title song, the synthesizer plays the main melody. Blauer Regen, by contrast, has no drums and sounds ambient. Sonnenrad was released together with Sterntaler on a single. Most critics reacted positively. Later Rother re-recorded Fontana di luna as Morning Sun, with the project Station 17.
werk/michael-rother-sterntaler.listen: Listen to Blauer Regen and notice how the music sounds without drums: what takes the place of the rhythm?

werk/midge-ure-breathe.text:
Breathe from 1996 was the fourth solo album by Midge Ure, the former frontman of Ultravox. Recording was finished in early 1995, in studios in Los Angeles, San Francisco, Dublin and in his own studio in Bath. The producer was Richard Feldman. He had first recorded four tracks with Julian Mendelsohn, but they were later done again. The record label left the album on the shelf for more than a year.

The origin lies in an American tour from 1992 with other songwriters. There he played Vienna on acoustic guitar and noticed that he could also make music without much electronics. Inspired by his Scottish background, he blended uilleann pipes and bodhrán with didgeridoo and Gaelic singing. At first the record sold poorly. Only when Swatch used the title track in a TV commercial did Breathe become a hit in several European countries in 1998, reaching number one in Italy and Austria.
werk/midge-ure-breathe.listen: Listen to Live Forever, a song inspired by the book Interview with the Vampire by Anne Rice, and consider whether you can hear that atmosphere.

werk/midge-ure-pure.text:
Pure was released on 16 September 1991 and was the third solo album by Midge Ure, the former frontman of Ultravox. It was his first record on a new label, BMG-Arista. For two years he gathered the material, in his home studio in London and in the basement of his house on the Caribbean island of Montserrat, after he had cleared up the damage from Hurricane Hugo. According to him, the central theme was the highs and lows of love.

The record opens with See Hope in the Morning Light, a blend of African rhythms and a gospel choir, supplemented by uilleann pipes from Paddy Moloney. The song was meant to be uplifting about life itself, not about religion or the afterlife. He wrote Let It Go? about people who think someone else will sort things out. Besides those two, Cold, Cold Heart was also released as a single. The album reached number 36 on the UK album chart.
werk/midge-ure-pure.listen: Listen to the opening track See Hope in the Morning Light and notice how the gospel choir and the uilleann pipes come together with African rhythms.

werk/midge-ure-the-gift.text:
Midge Ure made this album while his band Ultravox was taking a break. It was his first solo record. He recorded most of it in a new studio in his garden in Chiswick. For five tracks he worked with Danny Mitchell. Wastelands had originally already appeared in 1980 on an album by Modern Man. He dedicates the title song to the Scottish architect Charles Rennie Mackintosh.

Besides pop songs there are three instrumental pieces, recorded on the island of Montserrat with a Casio CZ-101. In Edo, Ure plays a koto, which he bought during a Japanese tour with Ultravox. He wanted to hear the sound of scratching fingers on the strings and therefore did not use a synthesizer. The single If I Was reached number one in the British chart and the album reached number two.
werk/midge-ure-the-gift.listen: In Edo, listen to the koto: notice the sound of the fingers on the strings, which Ure deliberately wanted to preserve.

werk/mike-oldfield-hergest-ridge.text:
After the unexpected success of Tubular Bells in 1973, Mike Oldfield did not want to tour and avoided the press. He withdrew to Hergest Ridge, a hill on the border of England and Wales, and wrote the follow-up there. He recorded it in 1974 at The Manor in Oxfordshire, again with Tom Newman as co-producer. Like the debut, it is a single composition in two parts, with changing moods and styles. Oldfield layers many tracks of electric guitar on top of one another, with a sustained, organ-like sound, and uses the voice as an instrument for texture. The sleeve shows the landscape of the hill.

The album spent three weeks at number one in England, until Tubular Bells displaced it from that spot. Oldfield himself felt it was a more considered work than his debut, even though the recording was hurried. Critics found it less inspired than its predecessor.
werk/mike-oldfield-hergest-ridge.listen: Listen to Hergest Ridge, Pt. 1 and notice how layers of guitar pile up and sometimes sound like an organ. Can you also hear voices used as an instrument?

werk/mike-oldfield-incantations.text:
Incantations is Mike Oldfield's fourth studio album and was released on 1 December 1978 on Virgin Records. After Ommadawn he moved to Bisley in Gloucestershire and built a new studio there, where he recorded from December 1977 to September 1978. He wanted to use real incantations, but ended up with folklore as a connecting thread, such as Diana the Huntress. For the first time he wrote string arrangements himself, and there is also flute. The words come from poems by Henry Longfellow and Ben Jonson.

The record became a double album in four parts, each taking up one side of an LP. Terry Riley was a major influence, especially through his use of ostinato. Oldfield called the double vibraphone section in part four the closest he ever came to self-expression. The album reached number 14 in the United Kingdom, his first outside the top five, and led to his first solo tour.
werk/mike-oldfield-incantations.listen: Listen to Incantations, Pt. Four and notice the section with two vibraphones and the electric guitar solo that follows it.

werk/mike-oldfield-ommadawn.text:
After Tubular Bells and Hergest Ridge, which was received more negatively, Mike Oldfield wanted to prove that he was more than a one-off success. He had his label install a twenty-four-track studio in his house The Beacon near Kington, where he recorded from January to September 1975. Shortly after the start his mother died. Later the recording tape came loose, forcing him to begin his first side again. The album is one composition in two parts. The Manor in Oxfordshire was used for the African drums. Part Two ends with On Horseback, a song about riding along Hergest Ridge. The title comes from an Irish phrase written down by Clodagh Simonds, in which the word idiot occurs.

The album reached number four in England and went gold within two months. One critic later praised the space that each of the themes is given.
werk/mike-oldfield-ommadawn.listen: Listen to Ommadawn, Pt. 1 and notice the two themes at the beginning: how are they given all the room to be heard, without being developed straight away?

werk/mike-oldfield-platinum.text:
Platinum was released on 23 November 1979 on Virgin Records and is Mike Oldfield's fifth studio album. For the first time, a record of his contains shorter songs and music by others. In the United States and Canada a modified version was released under the title Airborn.

The first side is a nineteen-minute title piece in four parts. Airborne later became the theme tune of the BBC children's quiz First Class. Charleston is a humorous piece with horns, wordless vocals and whispered scat. North Star/Platinum Finale contains a fragment of the composition North Star by Philip Glass: the choir comes from him, the melody does not. The second side has Punkadiddle, a parody of punk rock, and Gershwin's I Got Rhythm, reworked as a ballad. The Globe and Mail saw the music as a logical continuation of the material from Tubular Bells.
werk/mike-oldfield-platinum.listen: Listen to Charleston, Pt. Three: notice the horns and the wordless vocals, and hear how light and playful this section sounds after the more serious opening parts.

werk/mike-oldfield-tubular-bells.text:
Mike Oldfield was nineteen when recording began. As a teenager he played bass in Kevin Ayers's band and taught himself the instruments that were lying around in the studios. With a borrowed tape recorder he built up layers of music at home in London. This produced a long instrumental piece that he eventually recorded at The Manor Studio in Oxfordshire, paid for by Richard Branson, for the very first album on Virgin Records.

Oldfield played almost all the instruments himself, with thousands of corrections on the tape. The album consists of two long parts and combines progressive rock, folk and minimalism. At the end of the first part, Vivian Stanshall introduces the instruments one by one. Sales were slow to start, until the opening melody was heard in the film The Exorcist in December 1973. After that the album became known worldwide and brought Virgin great success. In 1975 it won a Grammy.
werk/mike-oldfield-tubular-bells.listen: In Part One: Finale, listen to how Vivian Stanshall announces the instruments one by one, and count how each instrument joins in.

werk/miles-davis-bitches-brew.text:
After In a Silent Way, Miles Davis wanted to go even further with electric instruments. From 19 to 21 August 1969 he recorded in Studio B of Columbia in New York, with a large group: his regular band, supplemented by, among others, Joe Zawinul, John McLaughlin, Larry Young, Lenny White, Don Alias, Juma Santos and Bennie Maupin. He gave the musicians only a tempo, a few chords and a mood. The rest had to come out of improvisation.

Producer Teo Macero cut and spliced the recordings into long pieces, with tape loops and echo. Pharaoh's Dance contains nineteen edits; Miles Runs the Voodoo Down is the only one not edited. The rhythm section consisted of two bassists, two to three drummers and several electric pianos at once. The first reactions were mixed. The album won a Grammy in 1971 and is now regarded as a forerunner of jazz rock.
werk/miles-davis-bitches-brew.listen: In Pharaoh's Dance, listen to the stop-start opening: it was built entirely in the studio from repeated snippets of recording.

werk/miles-davis-blue-moods.text:
Blue Moods was released in late 1955 on Debut Records, the label of Charles Mingus. Miles Davis plays trumpet in a small group with Mingus on bass, trombonist Britt Woodman, vibraphonist Teddy Charles and drummer Elvin Jones. Mingus wrote the arrangement of Alone Together; Teddy Charles arranged the other tracks.

The liner notes explain why the record is so short: the grooves were cut wider and deeper so that the range of the low notes was better reproduced. AllMusic calls the record an excellent example of Cool Jazz, even though not all the musicians belonged to that movement. The album later also found its way into Mingus's large Debut box set.
werk/miles-davis-blue-moods.listen: Listen to Alone Together and notice how the trumpet and the trombone move around each other above the calm accompaniment.

werk/miles-davis-collectors-items.text:
Collectors' Items brings together two sessions with largely different musicians. The first took place in 1953. Miles Davis then played with Sonny Rollins and Charlie Parker, who for contractual reasons was credited as Charlie Chan on tenor saxophone. According to him it was chaotic: Parker drank heavily and spoke condescendingly, and fell asleep after an argument. The recordings were left on the shelf for years. Meanwhile Parker died in 1955 and the trumpeter moved to Columbia in 1956.

Because he still had a contractual obligation to Prestige, in 1956 he recorded a second session so that there would be enough material for an album. Only Rollins returned. The new pianist Tommy Flanagan and bassist Paul Chambers had only just arrived in New York, and Art Taylor was on drums. Besides Compulsion, 'Round Midnight and two versions of The Serpent's Tooth, the album includes In Your Own Sweet Way, Vierd Blues and No Line.
werk/miles-davis-collectors-items.listen: Listen first to The Serpent's Tooth (Take 1) and then to Take 2. Try to hear how the two recordings of the same piece differ from each other.

werk/miles-davis-kind-of-blue.text:
In 1959 Miles Davis recorded this album in two sessions at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in New York. His sextet included John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley and Bill Evans, whom he called back for this project. Wynton Kelly played piano on Freddie Freeloader. There was almost no rehearsal: the musicians were given only sketches of scales and melody lines. The persistent legend that everything was recorded in one take is, incidentally, not true.

The music rests entirely on modality. After the title piece of Milestones from 1958, the trumpeter went further away from hard bop here. Each soloist was given a series of scales as a framework and thus more freedom for the melody. Many critics see the album as his best work and as one of the most influential records ever made. Several of the pieces grew into jazz standards, and in 2002 the Library of Congress added the album to the National Recording Registry.
werk/miles-davis-kind-of-blue.listen: In So What, listen to the structure: sixteen bars in the first mode, eight in the second and then eight again in the first. Notice how calm and open the piece remains, without hurried chord changes.

werk/miles-davis-on-the-corner.text:
After Bitches Brew and Jack Johnson, Miles Davis was criticised by the jazz world, which accused him of chasing commercial success. In early 1972 he conceived On the Corner as an attempt to win back a young black audience that had exchanged jazz for the funk of Sly Stone and James Brown. Karlheinz Stockhausen and the ideas of Ornette Coleman and arranger Paul Buckmaster also played a part. The recordings were made in June and July 1972, with changing musicians such as Michael Henderson, John McLaughlin, Chick Corea and Herbie Hancock.

The music consists of repeated drum and bass patterns over which Davis played his trumpet through a wah-wah pedal. Producer Teo Macero cut and spliced the recordings into compositions. No musicians are credited on the sleeve. On release the record sold poorly and was rejected by jazz critics. The verdict has since improved greatly: many listeners outside jazz call it innovative, a forerunner of funk, post-punk, electronica and hip hop.
werk/miles-davis-on-the-corner.listen: Listen to On the Corner and notice the constantly recurring rhythms of drums and bass and how the trumpet plays raggedly over them.

werk/miles-davis-sketches-of-spain.text:
The idea for Sketches of Spain arose when Miles Davis's wife took him to a performance by the flamenco dancer Roberto Iglesias. Afterwards he bought every flamenco record he could find in New York. Together with arranger Gil Evans, with whom he had worked before, he recorded the album between November 1959 and March 1960 at Columbia's 30th Street Studio.

The record is built around the second movement of Joaquín Rodrigo's guitar concerto Concierto de Aranjuez, which takes up almost half of the record. Evans adapted it into an almost symphonic sound world, in which Davis plays first on flugelhorn and later on trumpet. The remaining pieces are largely derived from Spanish folk music. The album is regarded as an example of third stream, a hybrid of jazz, classical music and world music. DownBeat wrote warmly about it, and Evans and Davis won a Grammy in 1961.
werk/miles-davis-sketches-of-spain.listen: In Concierto de Aranjuez (Adagio), listen to how the flugelhorn first plays the melody faithfully and how Gil Evans's orchestra then builds a darker world of its own around that melody.

werk/miles-davis-tutu.text:
Tutu is Miles Davis's tribute to Archbishop Desmond Tutu, the human rights activist and opponent of apartheid. Some of the tracks were first intended as a collaboration with Prince, but he dropped out. Davis then worked with bassist and multi-instrumentalist Marcus Miller, who wrote and arranged almost everything and played most of the instruments himself. Recording took place mainly at Capitol Studios in Los Angeles and Clinton Recording in New York. The music is strongly influenced by the R&B and funk of the mid-1980s, with many synthesizers, sequencers and drum machines.

The album was released on 29 September 1986 on Warner Bros. Records and divided critics. It attracted a young new audience, but many jazz lovers dropped away because of the drum machines and synthesizers. Others felt that the music gave his improvisations a fine setting. He won a Grammy for it.
werk/miles-davis-tutu.listen: Listen to Tomaas and notice the reggae-like beat and Marcus Miller's bass line. Hear how the trumpet and the soprano saxophone respond briefly to one another in turn.

werk/milt-jackson-ballads-en-blues.text:
Ballads & Blues came about from recordings made in early 1956 in New York and at the Van Gelder Studio in Hackensack, New Jersey. The album was released on Atlantic. Jackson plays vibraphone in varying line-ups, for example with John Lewis on piano, Oscar Pettiford on bass and Kenny Clarke on drums. On the last three tracks tenor saxophonist Lucky Thompson also plays.

The repertoire contains standards by Cole Porter, Duke Ellington and Irving Berlin, among others, supplemented by Jackson's own compositions. The reception was glowing. The Penguin Guide to Jazz spoke of near-perfect Jackson, with the others giving him space. Allmusic gave four and a half stars and Billboard expected that fans would appreciate the horn session.
werk/milt-jackson-ballads-en-blues.listen: Listen to Solitude, a song by Duke Ellington, and notice how the vibraphone makes the melody sing.

werk/milt-jackson-milt-jackson-quartet.text:
Milt Jackson Quartet, also released as Soul Pioneers, contains recordings that vibraphonist Milt Jackson made on 20 May 1955 at the Van Gelder Studio in Hackensack, New Jersey. The album was released on Prestige. Jackson plays together with pianist Horace Silver, bassist Percy Heath and drummer Connie Kay, a small line-up in which every musician remains audible.

The record consists of six tracks, three on each side. You will find standards such as My Funny Valentine, The Nearness of You and I Should Care, alongside Stonewall, an original composition by Jackson. The AllMusic writer Scott Yanow called the music a pleasant set in a straightforward jazz style.
werk/milt-jackson-milt-jackson-quartet.listen: Listen to My Funny Valentine and notice how the vibraphone plays the familiar theme.

werk/milt-jackson-opus-de-jazz.text:
Opus de Jazz is an album by vibraphonist Milt Jackson, recorded in New York on 28 October 1955 and released on Savoy. The subtitle names the instrumentation: flute, vibraphone, piano, bass and drums. Frank Wess plays flute and, on one track, tenor saxophone, Hank Jones piano, Eddie Jones bass and Kenny Clarke drums.

The album contains four long tracks. Opus de Funk by Horace Silver is the longest at just over thirteen minutes. Ozzie Cadena wrote Opus Pocus and Opus and Interlude, and You Leave Me Breathless is by Ralph Freed and Frederick Hollander. Scott Yanow of Allmusic found it not essential, but pleasant music.
werk/milt-jackson-opus-de-jazz.listen: Listen to Opus de Funk and notice the difference in sound between the vibraphone and the flute.

werk/miriam-makeba-an-evening-with-belaf.text:
Despite the title, An Evening with Belafonte/Makeba is not a live record but a studio album, released in 1965 by RCA Victor. In those years Harry Belafonte supported African artists and wanted to make African music known worldwide. Of the twelve tracks, he sings five, Miriam Makeba five, and they sing two together. The songs are in Xhosa, Zulu and other African languages.

Many of the songs are about the position of black South Africans under apartheid. Beware, Verwoerd! targets Hendrik Verwoerd, and To Those We Love names political prisoners such as Nelson Mandela. The album won a Grammy, sold well and made the singer better known in the United States. AllMusic called it a powerful album of traditional South African music.
werk/miriam-makeba-an-evening-with-belaf.listen: Listen to Beware, Verwoerd! and notice the singing: what can you hear of the tone of a protest song, even if you do not understand the language?

werk/miriam-makeba-the-voice-of-africa.text:
The Voice of Africa is the South African singer's fourth album, released in 1964 by RCA Victor. It reached number 122 on the American album chart. The record has twelve short tracks, each lasting between one and three minutes. She wrote Uyadela and Mamoriri herself, Nomthini with Alan Salinga and Qhude with Hugh Masekela, who on the album also plays trumpet, arranges and conducts.

There are also songs by other writers, such as Langa More by Zeph Nkabinde, Willow Song by Giuseppe Verdi and Le Fleuve. The accompaniment consists of three guitarists, a bassist, a drummer, an alto saxophonist and a trombonist. The album thus consists of short songs with a small band.
werk/miriam-makeba-the-voice-of-africa.listen: Listen to Qhude and notice her voice and what the band does around it, in a song of less than three minutes.

werk/miroslav-vitous-first-meeting.text:
First Meeting was recorded in May 1979 and released in January 1980 on ECM. The Czech bassist Miroslav Vitouš plays here in a quartet with reed player John Surman, pianist Kenny Kirkland and drummer Jon Christensen. Kirkland and Christensen together form the rhythm section. Surman plays soprano saxophone and bass clarinet, Vitouš himself the double bass.

All the compositions are by the bassist, and the record mainly shows his qualities as a writer and player. The AllMusic reviewer, David R. Adler, gave three stars and recommended the album, but noted that it is hard to find.
werk/miroslav-vitous-first-meeting.listen: Listen to Silver Lake and notice the interplay between Vitouš's double bass and John Surman's reed instruments.

werk/miroslav-vitous-infinite-search.text:
Infinite Search is the debut album by the Czech jazz bassist Miroslav Vitouš. It was released in 1970 on Embryo Records, with Herbie Mann as producer. He led a group with Joe Henderson on tenor saxophone, John McLaughlin on electric guitar, Herbie Hancock on electric piano and Jack DeJohnette on drums. On one track Joe Chambers plays the drums.

The same recordings later also came out under two other titles. In 1972 a remixed version was released as Mountain in the Clouds, with one extra track, Cérečka. The same version also came out as The Bass. In 2016 the journalist Paul Rigby wrote of the album that he was impressed by McLaughlin's improvisations, which fill every space like a school of fish.
werk/miroslav-vitous-infinite-search.listen: Listen to Infinite Search and notice how the bass takes the lead. Can you hear the guitar improvising in the space around it?

werk/missy-elliott-under-construction.text:
Under Construction is Missy Elliott's fourth studio album and was released on 12 November 2002 on Elektra Records. Producer Timbaland was responsible for most of the music, with additional work by, among others, Craig Brockman, Nisan Stewart and Errol McCalla. Elliott dedicated the album to Aaliyah, who died in August 2001, and to the victims of the attacks of 11 September.

The album looks back at old-school hip hop and sends it through a futuristic sound. Work It was the first single and reached number 2 on the US Hot 100. Gossip Folks followed as the second single. Critics praised the abrasive rhythms and the playful, often daring lyrics. Under Construction received Grammy nominations for Best Rap Album and Album of the Year and appears in the book 1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die.
werk/missy-elliott-under-construction.listen: Listen to Work It and notice how bare and rhythmic the production is, and how Elliott plays the beat with her voice.

werk/modern-jazz-quartet-concorde.text:
Concorde is an album by the Modern Jazz Quartet, recorded on 2 July 1955 in New York and released that same year as Prestige 7005. It is the first album with drummer Connie Kay, who replaced Kenny Clarke, and the group's first LP conceived for the long-playing format from the outset. The liner notes ask the listener to regard the record as a performance in one of the best jazz clubs in America.

Besides Kay, Milt Jackson plays vibraphone, John Lewis piano and Percy Heath bass. The repertoire runs from Ralph's New Blues and All of You to a Gershwin Medley and Lewis's title track. AllMusic called the transition between the drummers smooth and the Gershwin interpretations definitive.
werk/modern-jazz-quartet-concorde.listen: In Gershwin Medley, listen to how the four songs by George and Ira Gershwin are strung together without a break.

werk/modern-jazz-quartet-django.text:
Django was released as a long-playing record in 1956, but the recordings date from June 1953, December 1954 and January 1955. Prestige first released them on two smaller records. The first session took place in New York, the later ones in Hackensack, New Jersey, with Rudy Van Gelder as recording engineer. The Modern Jazz Quartet consists of Milt Jackson on vibraphone, John Lewis on piano, Percy Heath on bass and Kenny Clarke on drums.

Lewis wrote Django in memory of guitarist Django Reinhardt, and Delaunay's Dilemma is a cheerful homage to the jazz critic Charles Delaunay. La Ronde Suite gives each band member space. AllMusic found the variety of styles and performances hard to surpass.
werk/modern-jazz-quartet-django.listen: Listen to Django and notice how the vibraphone and the piano complement each other.

werk/morrissey-southpaw-grammar.text:
Southpaw Grammar was released on 28 August 1995 and is Morrissey's fifth solo album. It came out on RCA in the United Kingdom and on Reprise in the United States. Steve Lillywhite produced. The record sounds different from his earlier work: two tracks last more than ten minutes, The Operation opens with a drum solo of almost two and a half minutes by Spencer Cobrin, and there is a sample of a Shostakovich symphony. The sleeve features the boxer Kenny Lane.

AllMusic called it his art rock album, with strings, drum solos and two ten-minute tracks. The singles were Dagenham Dave and The Boy Racer. In the press the reception was mostly positive, but Q wrote that it would earn more respect than sales. Later some saw it as the moment when the general public turned away from him, whereas Stereogum called it his high point.
werk/morrissey-southpaw-grammar.listen: Listen to The Operation and notice the drum solo with which the song opens and what comes in afterwards.

werk/morrissey-vauxhall-and-i.text:
Vauxhall and I is Morrissey's fourth solo album and was released in March 1994 on Parlophone in Great Britain. Chris Dickie and Steve Lillywhite produced the record. The band consisted of Alain Whyte and Boz Boorer on guitar, Jonny Bridgewood on bass and Woodie Taylor on drums. In Spring-Heeled Jim, snippets of dialogue from a documentary about a youth club in south London can be heard. At the end of Billy Budd, a line from the 1948 film Oliver Twist is heard.

The record was a success. It reached the top of the British chart and made the top twenty in America. The first single, The More You Ignore Me, The Closer I Get, reached number 8 in Great Britain and became the only song by the singer or by The Smiths to chart high in America. Q magazine placed the record in the best ten of 1994. Pitchfork later called it his first truly mature solo record, and the NME his best.
werk/morrissey-vauxhall-and-i.listen: Listen to Billy Budd and notice the line from an old film at the end of the song.

werk/motley-crue-girls-girls-girls.text:
Girls, Girls, Girls is Mötley Crüe's fourth studio album, released on 20 May 1987. It was the last collaboration with producer Tom Werman, who had also made Shout at the Devil and Theatre of Pain. The record took on a blues rock-influenced sound, which was positively received. The singles are Girls, Girls, Girls and You're All I Need, and Wild Side became an MTV favourite.

Mick Mars's guitar sits more clearly at the front of the mix than on Theatre of Pain, wrote The Georgia Straight. That paper heard in Dancing on Glass, Five Years Dead and the title track something of the excitement of the debut, with a guitar riff in the spirit of Aerosmith. Ultimate Classic Rock called Wild Side one of the band's most complex compositions. The album reached number two on the Billboard 200 and went four times platinum.
werk/motley-crue-girls-girls-girls.listen: Listen to Girls, Girls, Girls and notice the guitar riff that carries the song.

werk/motley-crue-shout-at-the-devil.text:
The band's second album was released in September 1983 and became their breakthrough. Just before the recording, the group played five shows as the opening act for Kiss. During the sessions Nikki Sixx was in a serious car accident, after which he became addicted to painkillers and later to heroin. The pentagram on the sleeve came from the theatrical band Sister, in which Sixx had previously played with Blackie Lawless. Lawless gave him permission to use the imagery.

The album sold two hundred thousand copies in two weeks and made Mötley Crüe one of the best-selling metal bands of the 1980s. The singles Looks That Kill, Too Young to Fall in Love and Shout at the Devil were modest hits. The title and the pentagram earned the band a place in a TV item about Christian groups concerned about Satanism.
werk/motley-crue-shout-at-the-devil.listen: In the title song Shout at the Devil, listen to the chorus that you can shout along to, and notice how dark the song sounds.

werk/motley-crue-theatre-of-pain.text:
Theatre of Pain is Mötley Crüe's third studio album, released on 21 June 1985. Recording began in January 1985 under a dark cloud: singer Vince Neil was on trial after a car accident in which Nicholas Dingley of Hanoi Rocks was killed, and bassist Nikki Sixx was struggling with a heroin addiction. Tom Werman produced again. The record marks the shift from the hard metal sound of Shout at the Devil to glam metal.

Smokin' in the Boys Room, a cover of Brownsville Station, gave the band its first top 20 hit. Home Sweet Home came about when Neil sang along to a piano lick that Tommy Lee played in the studio. The critics were negative and some band members do not think highly of it either, but the album reached number six on the American chart and went four times platinum.
werk/motley-crue-theatre-of-pain.listen: Listen to Home Sweet Home and notice the role of the piano in this power ballad.

werk/motley-crue-too-fast-for-love.text:
This debut was released in November 1981 in a first pressing of nine hundred copies on the band's own label, Leathür Records. The first recordings were made half a year after the first gig at the Starwood in Hollywood. The band then signed with Elektra. The album was remixed under the supervision of Roy Thomas Baker and partly re-recorded. That version from August 1982, with a different running order, became the standard version. Stick to Your Guns was dropped from it.

The first reviews were mixed. Many critics found the music derivative and criticised the playing and the singing, although some did like the speed and the rawness. Later assessments were considerably more favourable. AllMusic wrote that the band sounds like a bar band making up for what it lacks in technique with enthusiasm. In the United States the record reached number 77 and later went platinum after all.
werk/motley-crue-too-fast-for-love.listen: In Live Wire, listen to the fast tempo and the raw, unpolished playing of the band.

werk/motorhead-1916.text:
In 1990 Lemmy moved from England to West Hollywood. Recording for 1916, Motörhead's ninth album, began with producer Ed Stasium, but the band fired him when he added claves and tambourines to Going to Brazil without consultation. Peter Solley took over. The album was released in January 1991, the first on WTG Records, and was the last with Phil Taylor on all tracks.

The title track is a slow ballad about soldiers killed in the First World War, inspired by the Battle of the Somme, and leans on keyboards. There are also hard-hitting rock tracks such as I'm So Bad (Baby I Don't Care) and Ramones, a tribute to the punk band. Critics reacted mostly positively, including in Rolling Stone, and Robert Christgau gave an A minus.
werk/motorhead-1916.listen: Listen to 1916 and notice how little is going on beneath the vocals: Lemmy is only sparingly accompanied, unlike on the rest of the album.

werk/motorhead-march-or-die.text:
After the success of 1916, Motörhead received a second contract with Sony. Lemmy had meanwhile written four songs for Ozzy Osbourne's No More Tears, which earned him a lot of money. For March ör Die, released in July 1992, the band again worked with producer Pete Solley. During the recording, drummer Phil Taylor left. As a result three drummers can be heard on the album: Taylor, Tommy Aldridge and Mikkey Dee, who later became a permanent member.

Ozzy Osbourne sings on I Ain't No Nice Guy, on which Slash of Guns N' Roses also plays guitar. Slash can also be heard on You Better Run. According to Lemmy, the song reached number 10 on the radio charts, despite little support from Sony. The reviews were mixed: AllMusic was critical, while Entertainment Weekly felt that the album went beyond ordinary heavy metal.
werk/motorhead-march-or-die.listen: Listen to I Ain't No Nice Guy and notice how Ozzy Osbourne's voice blends with Lemmy's, and Slash's guitar work.

werk/muddy-waters-after-the-rain.text:
After the Rain was released in 1969 as Muddy Waters's sixth studio album and is the follow-up to Electric Mud from the year before. Many of the same musicians played on it, including Phil Upchurch, Pete Cosey, Charles Stepney, Louis Satterfield and Morris Jennings. Marshall Chess, Stepney and Gene Barge produced the record.

Unlike its predecessor, it consists mainly of the singer's own songs, and his own guitar playing comes clearly to the fore again. The music remains distorted, but is less emphatically psychedelic. Bottom of the Sea appears only on this album. Commercially the record did worse than Electric Mud and it did not enter the Billboard 200. An AllMusic reviewer felt that it sounded more as you would expect from him, and a later review called the second half solid Chicago blues with slide guitar.
werk/muddy-waters-after-the-rain.listen: Listen to Bottom of the Sea, the track that appears only on this album, and notice what remains of the blues beneath the distorted guitars.

werk/muddy-waters-electric-mud.text:
Electric Mud came about in 1968 from an idea of producer Marshall Chess, who wanted to let a younger audience that loved psychedelic rock hear the music of Muddy Waters. Chess brought together the most adventurous jazz-rock musicians in Chicago, including Pete Cosey, Phil Upchurch and Charles Stepney, and had them play with wah-wah pedal, fuzzbox, organ and saxophone. It was the bluesman's fifth studio album, recorded with members of Rotary Connection instead of his own band.

(I'm Your) Hoochie Coochie Man sounds here with free jazz influences and a concert harp, and Let's Spend the Night Together by the Rolling Stones became a gospel-style soul version. The record sold 150,000 copies in six weeks and was his first album on the American charts. Blues purists and American critics, however, considered it a mockery of the blues, whereas in England it was better received. He himself was not keen on it, because he could not play this music live.
werk/muddy-waters-electric-mud.listen: Listen to Let's Spend the Night Together and notice how a Rolling Stones rock song acquires a gospel-like soul colour here, with heavy guitar and organ.
